full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN, with medium confidence.** The system is the standard Keller–Segel-type chemotaxis model used for Budrene–Berg E. coli patterns. The model has cells, a self-secreted attractant, and a consumed nutrient that cells also follow. A uniform state is unstable, so it coarsens into spots or blobs.

**1. Model family.** This is chemotaxis pattern formation, a reaction–diffusion–advection system. It is a Keller–Segel model with these features:
- Attractant production and decay.
- Nutrient consumption and resupply.
- Taxis toward both the attractant and the nutrient.
- A saturating sensitivity, b/(1+b²), which is volume-filling or receptor-saturation type.

**2. The behaviour.** Cells start nearly uniform and spontaneously form localized dense blobs. The Moran's I of 0.977 and the large standard deviation of 2.3 mean strong spatial structure, and the mean stays at 1 because cell number is conserved. This is the self-trapping or chemotactic collapse instability. Local accumulation raises local attractant, which draws in more cells.

**3. Sources I checked.**
- Brenner, Levitov & Budrene (1998), "Physical Mechanisms for Chemotactic Pattern Formation by Bacteria", *Biophysical Journal* 74(4), 1677–1693. The Harvard Brenner group page confirms title, authors, year and venue. It is the earliest clear theory source in my results. I did not read its text, so I am relying on its title and its frequent citation as the standard theory of this pattern formation. It builds on the experiments of Budrene & Berg, *Nature* 349, 630 (1991) and *Nature* 376, 49 (1995). Both are confirmed as reference entries in the search results.
- Physica D 395 (2019), 24–36. This is a Keller–Segel model in which cells make a chemoattractant and also move along a nutrient gradient they create by consuming it. It treats the pulse-like patterns as a Turing-type instability. The search result did not show the full title or authors, so I can't give a full citation.
- Chemotactic Sensing towards Ambient and Secreted Attractant Drives Collective Behaviour of E. coli, *PLoS ONE* 2013, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0074878. It is a particle-based model with secreted attractant, nutrient consumption and nutrient taxis. The essential mechanism is a self-trapping feedback: local accumulation raises attractant secretion, which draws in more bacteria. It also reports that when nutrient-gradient sensitivity is doubled, spots no longer form in the wake of the advancing ring. Its authors are not shown in the snippet.
- Review: Brenner, "Chemotactic patterns without chemotaxis", *PNAS* 107(26), 11653–11654 (2010). This is a commentary on the field. The chemotaxis coefficient and pattern-formation context are confirmed in the result.

**4. Caveats.**
- I did not find a paper using exactly this b/(1+b²) sensitivity together with a uniformly resupplied nutrient in a 2D periodic box. Equivalent saturating or volume-filling Keller–Segel forms are widely studied, so I doubt the difference matters.
- Nutrient taxis here is stronger than attractant taxis (14 vs 11.1). The 2013 PLoS ONE particle model suggests strong nutrient sensing can suppress spots in a growing colony. That is a different setting, with growth and a moving front. My results don't show whether a closed periodic box behaves the same way.
- The mix of aggregates and mobile blobs in the simulation could depend on the parameters. I did not check the linear-stability threshold.
